To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the rate of cooling of carcasses is controlled by the rate of heat loss from the carcass to the air, which in turn is controlled by the thermal resistance of the meat surface and by the air speed and temperature.

the chilling rate of beef carcass halves is a linear function of the air temperature difference across the surface of the carcass and the surface area of the carcass, and that the chilling of beef carcass sides can be predicted using a model which includes the effects of carcass weight, the surface area of fat and lean tissue and the air temperature difference between the carcass surface and the air.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is still a great deal to be learned about the chilling process, particularly in relation to meat quality and microbiological control.
there is still much research to be done, but there is also much to be learned from the papers presented in this volume.
the meat chilling and distribution industry has changed significantly during the last 20 years.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
meat chilling and distribution is now a mature science, but that there are many areas where research and development work is still required.
we are now much better informed on the physical processes involved in meat chilling and the effects on quality and safety.
the industry is now more efficient in its chilling operations and that the industry is more concerned with the quality of the product than with the quantity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of the term “meat” is a misnomer because the meat is not the only component in meat products.
the use of a single, uniform standard to evaluate the safety of all food products is impractical and may be misleading.

the meat industry needs to focus on the following: (a) the use of the most appropriate chilling methods for each type of carcass; (b) the need for more research on the effects of chilling methods on meat quality and safety; (c) the need for research into the effects of chilling on the microbiological safety of meat and meat products; and (d) the need to develop more rapid methods for the microbiological assessment of chilled meat and meat products.
